title: TSV erasure coding replaces HBM spare TSVs and repair
idea: Ideal: TSV defects do not matter. Closest: data across the 1024-bit HBM interface is Reed-Solomon coded in lane groups (e.g., 8 parity lanes per 128), so open or resistive TSVs are corrected on the fly as erasures instead of being repaired with spares and fuses at test.
why: Fact 6: recovers part of the 20-30% stack yield loss and permits finer TSV pitch with higher defect rates for ~6% lane overhead.

title: Nantero NRAM's random-fabric variability replaced by crossed aligned nanotube bilayers
idea: Nantero's NRAM spent two decades unshipped at scale partly because spin-coated random CNT fabric gave cell-to-cell differences in junction count and switching. Fix: deposit two layers of pre-aligned, sorted nanotubes crossed at 90 degrees (Langmuir-Schaefer or floating evaporative assembly) so every cell contains the same number of tube-tube junctions.
why: Van-der-Waals-latched, zero-refresh cell with a tight distribution, removing verify loops and spare overhead; BEOL-compatible and radiation hard.

title: Substitute battery ride-through rules with NV-state credits for telecom sites
idea: Policy: let cell sites and critical infrastructure meet backup mandates (e.g., multi-hour battery rules) with fewer battery hours if their compute uses certified non-volatile working memory that resumes state instantly.
why: Creates a guaranteed early market for U.S.-made NV DRAM-class memory and cuts lithium battery demand; drives volume and cost-down learning.

title: NEMS relay access switches give zero-leakage tiny storage nodes
idea: Effect: electrostatic actuation of nano-electromechanical relays. The access transistor becomes an electrostatically actuated beam with a ~10 nm gap, and the air gap in the off state means no subthreshold or junction leakage, so a 0.1 fF parasitic node holds data far beyond 64 ms; the relays are metal-only and low-temperature, so they stack in BEOL.
why: 10x density: about 10 BEOL layers of 4F^2 crosspoint relays over CMOS periphery give ~10x. Same cost: metal deposition and no EUV. The reliability risk is contact wear against DRAM-level endurance (~1e15 cycles).

title: Hammer-proof legacy tier for page tables and keys
idea: Ideal: hammering cannot hurt what matters. Closest: page tables, kernel structures and crypto keys live in a small 180 nm DRAM or SRAM tier whose wide cell spacing makes it physically immune to row hammer, so the dense main memory can drop costly TRR to cheap probabilistic neighbor refresh backed by ordinary ECC.
why: Fact 9: removes the privilege-escalation risk that forces aggressive mitigation; recovers ~5-10% of main-memory bandwidth and refresh energy.

title: Molybdenum-filled TSVs match silicon expansion, shrinking stress zones
idea: TRIZ #37 Thermal expansion: through-silicon vias are filled with domestic molybdenum (CTE ~5 ppm/K, near silicon's ~3) instead of copper (~17), removing the thermomechanical stress that degrades retention of nearby cells and forces keep-out zones.
why: Shrinks keep-out area and stress-related retention tails near TSVs, reclaiming part of the HBM area tax (fact 6) with no imported fill metal; Mo's higher resistivity is tolerable over 30-50 um vias.

title: Exascale ABFT: checksum rows riding inside weight matrices
idea: Million-core supercomputers use Huang-Abraham algorithm-based fault tolerance. Append a checksum row and column to every weight and activation tile, so each GEMM on the accelerator detects and corrects single corrupted elements in the operands it just read from HBM, for ~1-3% extra FLOPs. HBM devices and protocol are untouched.
why: End-to-end correction covers weak on-die ECC, so accelerators can use lower-grade HBM dies or switch off sideband ECC and reclaim its ~3-12% of capacity and bandwidth (facts 5, 6).

title: Voltage-accelerated room-temperature retention test replaces fluid-chilled testers
idea: Reverse the stress axis: instead of heating and chilling test heads with perfluoropolyether heat-transfer fluids, retention screening runs at room temperature with raised cell-node, plate and negative-wordline bias that accelerates junction and GIDL leakage by a calibrated factor equivalent to 85-95 C.
why: Removes PFAS fluids from ATE and cuts thermal soak time ~5x, lowering test capital per bit.

title: OLED burn-in ledger that trims subarray wordline voltages over life
idea: OLED drivers count the cumulative on-time of each pixel and boost the aged pixels. The DRAM would accumulate the activation-time integral of each subarray in a small counter. Local regulators then trim that subarray's VPP and negative-wordline level to track the access-transistor Vth drift from BTI/HCI, so the full end-of-life guardband is not applied from day one.
why: This recovers ~100-200 mV of lifetime guardband against the voltage floor (fact 10): about 10-15% wordline energy, or a tighter leakage tail early in life.

title: Core-stack thermistor compensation revived: temperature-tracking negative wordline bias
idea: Core memories put thermistors in the stack to retune drive currents as ferrite properties drifted with temperature. Each subarray sets its negative wordline-low voltage and body bias from a local temperature sensor and replica leakage cells that find, in real time, the minimum of subthreshold leakage plus GIDL (which moves with temperature), instead of using one worst-case bias.
why: Water and leakage tail (fact 3): holding the hot leakage tail ~3x lower lets DRAM run 10-15 C hotter at the same refresh rate, removing the need for chilled or evaporative cooling (>10x less water with dry coolers).

title: Thermostat wordline: off-voltage tracks temperature to the leakage minimum
idea: At each temperature the access transistor's total leakage (subthreshold vs GIDL) has a minimum at a specific negative wordline voltage; an on-die sensor and table steer VNWL from about -0.2 V at 25 C to about -0.5 V at 125 C, re-trimmed yearly to follow aging.
why: Fact 3 under 125 C for 10 years: ~2-4x lower hot leakage than a fixed VNWL, halving hot refresh while avoiding the constant GIDL field that accelerates oxide wear.

title: Negative wordline shake pulses lock traps into low-leak state
idea: Worse: leave variable-retention-time traps free to jump between high- and low-leak states unpredictably. Flip: periodically apply a short, strongly negative wordline and positive body pulse that empties or fills the metastable gate-edge traps into their low-leakage configuration, shrinking VRT-driven tail jumps.
why: Fact 3: VRT is why retention profiling is unreliable; taming it would let row-level adaptive refresh work safely, cutting refresh 3-5x.

title: Reverse-bias healing pulses empty traps during idle periods
idea: Timescale shift (seconds of stress -> milliseconds of recovery): during idle self-refresh windows, drive negative wordline and reverse storage-node bias pulses that detrap charge accumulated at the access-transistor interface, like NBTI recovery in logic.
why: Shrinks the aged leakage tail and the hammer susceptibility that grows over years, possibly holding retention near the time-zero distribution.

title: RAIDR's VRT killer exposed by accelerated trap-toggle burn-in screening
idea: Multi-rate refresh (RAIDR) died because Variable Retention Time cells jump between strong and weak bins after profiling. Fix exactly that at test: a burn-in recipe alternating high temperature, negative-wordline and GIDL-stress phases forces trap occupancy to toggle hundreds of times in minutes, so VRT-prone cells reveal themselves and are fused to spare rows before binning.
why: Makes retention-binned refresh safe: 2-4x longer refresh interval for >99.9% of rows, cutting the ~46 fJ/bit refresh tax and 10-20% bandwidth loss (fact 3).

title: Per-row trimmed negative wordline for tail rows only
idea: Ideal: zero off-state leakage. Closest: each row gets a 2-bit trim register set at test that picks its standby wordline voltage from -0.2/-0.4/-0.6 V, so rows holding tail cells get deep negative bias (~10x lower subthreshold leakage) while healthy rows stay shallow and avoid the GIDL penalty of deep bias.
why: Fact 3: cuts the leakage of the rows that set refresh by ~10x; refresh interval 2-4x longer at ~1% area.

title: No external sensors: ECC syndrome servo trims bias and refresh
idea: Imposed limit: no added test or sense hardware. On-die ECC correction counts per bank feed a closed-loop controller that continuously adjusts the negative wordline voltage, VARY trim and refresh interval to hold a target corrected-error rate (~1e-9). The ECC syndromes are the sensor.
why: Removes worst-case guardbands set for corner temperature and the worst die. Average refresh interval ~2x longer and wordline stress lower.

title: MeV-implant proximity gettering under the array
idea: Ideal: silicon with no metal impurities near the storage node. Closest: a high-energy (MeV) carbon or silicon implant places a damage layer ~2-3 um below the array that traps iron, nickel and copper during later anneals, removing the deep-level generation centers behind tail cells.
why: Fact 3: shrinks the defect-driven tail, possibly 2-4x longer worst-case retention, using 1990s MeV implanters.

title: NbO2 Mott tripwire integrates row activations, fires neighbor refresh
idea: Effect: Mott insulator-metal transition. Each wordline strap gets a tiny RC node that receives a fixed charge packet per activation and leaks with a ~64 ms time constant; an NbO2 threshold switch (Mott transition ~800 C, so stable at 95 C, unlike VO2) across the node snaps metallic once the node crosses ~0.6 V (about N activations within the window) and pulses a refresh-request line for the two neighboring rows. The result is an analog, self-decaying per-row counter of ~100 nm^2 with no SRAM tracker tables.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): deterministic per-row detection at ~1k-activation thresholds, immune to many-sided tracker-evasion patterns; replaces CAM/SRAM trackers in the periphery (~5-10x less mitigation area) and removes probabilistic over-refresh.

title: Mg: MgO stochastic tunnel junctions as coin-flip hammer counters
idea: A BEOL MgO magnetic tunnel junction beside each row driver gets a sub-critical pulse on every activation, switching with probability ~1/500 from thermal noise; a switched junction triggers neighbor refresh and is reset, giving a hardware probabilistic counter with no tables and no attacker-predictable state.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) protection below 1k-activation thresholds with near-zero periphery area (fact 7) and true randomness for free.

title: Etch slow to leak less: chlorine atomic-layer channel recess
idea: Reverse the throughput priority: the recessed-channel access transistor trench is cut by self-limiting Cl2/Ar atomic-layer etching, one monolayer per cycle, instead of fast fluorine plasma, flattening channel depth variation to ~1 nm.
why: Tighter Vt and lower trench-corner field compress the leakage tail ~2x so refresh can relax; slower etch adds tool time but zero fluorine.

title: Desert solar thermal swings: thermal-cycling screen flushes out VRT cells
idea: Desert electronics see 50 C daily swings that expose latent defects. Add a fast package test that cycles dies between -10 C and 95 C several times while repeatedly retention-testing them, pushing variable-retention-time cells into their leaky state so they are repaired before shipment. Nothing at the interface changes.
why: VRT cells escape single-pass tests and later force fleet-wide conservative refresh. Catching them early cuts field errors and supports ~1.5x looser refresh guardbands (fact 3).

title: Soft-decision sense amps feed LDPC, accepting 40% smaller capacitors
idea: Worse: force every sense amp to make a hard 0/1 call and throw away how close the call was. Flip: add a second offset-biased latch per sense-amp group that outputs a 1-bit confidence flag with each bit, and run a soft-decision LDPC code in the controller (as NAND does), which corrects far more raw errors per parity bit than hard BCH.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: soft decoding tolerates raw BER ~1e-4 instead of ~1e-9, letting Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~3 fF and capacitor AR from ~70:1 to ~45:1, a cheaper etch with higher yield.

title: Hydrogen-rich silicon nitride reservoir continuously re-passivates interface traps
idea: Worse: run one forming-gas anneal and let hydrogen leave interface dangling bonds over the product's life, so leakage tails creep up. Flip: deposit a hydrogen-loaded SiN:H / a-Si:H reservoir near the access transistors with a diffusion barrier above, so slow H release keeps re-passivating newly broken Si/SiO2 bonds at operating temperature.
why: Fact 3 tail aging: a self-healing interface (Si, N, H only) holds retention near time-zero, cutting end-of-life refresh guardband ~2x.

title: Long-context KV triage: low-attention tokens live on relaxed-refresh ranks
idea: Million-token KV caches are among the most extreme memory users. Track each token's cumulative attention score and migrate the bottom ~70% of tokens' K/V blocks onto ranks the controller runs at 4x longer tREFI, or onto retention-weak binned DIMMs. High-attention tokens stay on standard ranks, and errors in rarely attended tokens barely move outputs.
why: The KV cache dominates long-context serving memory. Relaxing refresh on most of it saves refresh power and bandwidth and creates demand for weak bins (fact 3).

title: Exascale checkpoint inside DRAM: RowClone shadow rows for rollback
idea: Exascale machines survive frequent faults through checkpoints. Add an in-DRAM SNAPSHOT command that copies a row to a shadow row in a reserved subarray by bitline copy (~90 ns, no bus traffic). When an uncorrectable error hits, the runtime rolls back to the shadow copy instead of killing the job.
why: Detected-uncorrectable errors become cheap rollbacks, so DRAM can run weaker codes or cells at higher uncorrectable rates, and checkpoint traffic to NVMe shrinks (facts 5, 8).

title: Earth-abundant DRAM grade standard with mandatory host ECC
idea: Worse: write qualification standards so strict that only W/Hf/Ru-based processes can pass. Flip: create a JEDEC and U.S. procurement 'EA-grade' spec that allows ~100x higher raw BER and longer retention tails if the module ships with a defined host-side ECC plus adaptive refresh, explicitly so Hf/W/Ru/Co-free cells become buyable.
why: Scarce-resource intensity and U.S. manufacturability: opens a market for abundant-element fabs where reliability comes from architecture, trading ~3-6% parity for chokepoint independence.

title: Ferroelectric remnant in capacitor gives LDPC a second opinion
idea: Box [medium: Hf/Zr-oxide capacitor with a tuned small ferroelectric remnant | access: standard | sense: dual-mode charge + polarization | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: ALD]. The bit is stored as charge, but each write also nudges a weak, slowly relaxing polarization; when ECC fails, a second polarization read supplies a likelihood value per bit so LDPC soft decoding recovers words that hard decoding cannot.
why: Facts 1/3: a free, physically independent second copy lets smaller-Cs or leakier cells pass; ~10x lower uncorrectable rate at equal raw BER.

title: Electro-optic imaging maps every cell's retention at wafer sort
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: standard | sense: optical, via removable electro-optic polymer film | integration: wafer-level test | substrate: bulk | fab: temporary spin-on film]. At sort a removable Pockels-effect film over the array is imaged with polarized light while cells decay, capturing every cell's leakage curve in seconds; the per-die map is fused on chip to drive repair and per-row refresh classes.
why: Facts 3/4: replaces hours of electrical retention testing with seconds of imaging and enables shipping weak dies with exact maps; ~5% more sellable dies.

title: ReRAM CAM repairs individual failing bits in the field
idea: Box [medium: capacitor + side ReRAM CAM | access: standard | sense: standard + CAM match | integration: monolithic BEOL | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. A 64k-entry ReRAM content-addressable table in the periphery stores failing-cell addresses found by boot-time BIST and supplies the replacement bit on a match, dropping repair granularity from whole rows or columns to single bits.
why: Yield and Fact 3: dies with ~1e-5 scattered weak cells ship and tail cells are repaired instead of driving refresh; ~5-10% die-yield recovery.

title: HBM stack RAID with a parity die and live rebuild
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: 12-high HBM stack | substrate: bulk | fab: standard]. One die of a 12-high stack holds XOR/RS parity across the other 11, so a die with dead TSVs, a failed bank or a hammer-corrupted row is reconstructed on the fly instead of scrapping the whole stack.
why: Fact 6: converts 20-30% stack yield loss into ~8% capacity overhead and ships stacks that fail today.

title: JEDEC relaxed-retention DRAM grade with mandatory host chipkill
idea: Box [policy layer over medium: capacitor | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: DIMM | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. Standardize a DRAM grade with 16 ms base retention, readable per-bank retention-class registers and mandatory host chipkill, so fabs can ship dies that fail the 64 ms spec as standard parts.
why: Supply and yield: +5-10% usable output per wafer and a faster yield ramp for new U.S. fabs.

title: Layer recompute replaces ECC for AI training activations
idea: Box [medium: ECC-free cheap DRAM | access: standard | sense: 32-bit CRC per tile | integration: accelerator HBM | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. Activations saved for the backward pass go into ECC-less, relaxed-refresh memory with a CRC per tile; a mismatch triggers recomputation of that layer from the last checkpoint, which costs <1% compute at observed error rates.
why: Reliability tax: drops 12.5% ECC overhead and lets ~2x weaker memory hold 40-60% of the training footprint.

title: Refresh-time 2D parity scrubbing computed inside sense amplifiers
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: standard | sense: sense amps with XOR accumulator latch | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. During each refresh sweep the sense amps XOR every refreshed row into a column-parity latch and compare it with a stored parity row (updated by write deltas), while per-row parity bits flag the row, so the row-column intersection locates and fixes single flips at zero extra activations.
why: Facts 3/9: turns refresh into scrubbing that catches retention and hammer flips before they accumulate, with no extra bandwidth.

title: Energy-grade DRAM bins sold against a contracted raw BER
idea: Box [medium: any | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: hyperscaler-owned host decoder | substrate: bulk | fab: existing fabs]. Fabs test each die for the lowest VARY/VPP that meets a contracted raw BER (e.g., 1e-5) instead of zero errors and sell it as an 'E-grade' part priced per pJ/access to buyers who run strong host codes.
why: Constraint: many dies reach 0.45-0.5 V at 1e-5 BER, ~5-10x lower CV^2 per access; monetizes margin that zero-error specs throw away.

title: JEDEC soft-information pins export per-read confidence to hosts
idea: Box [medium: any | access: standard | sense: sense amp with margin comparator | integration: standard DIMM | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. A JEDEC standard adds one confidence bit per 8 data bits, set when the sense differential fell below a guard threshold, so host decoders treat low-confidence bits as erasures and arrays can run at much lower voltage.
why: Constraint: erasure decoding roughly doubles correctable errors at equal parity, letting VARY drop ~2.5x (~6-10x CV^2); a policy that unlocks it industry-wide.

title: Halve the EUV dose; stochastic misprints become erasures
idea: Po: print the chip blurry. EUV dose on critical DRAM layers is cut 40-50%, raising scanner throughput ~1.5-1.8x, and the resulting rise in stochastic missing or bridged contacts (~0.1-1% of cells) is mapped at test as stuck cells, which as erasures cost about half the redundancy of random errors.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital (fact 4): the same scanner fleet patterns ~50% more wafer layers; ~5-8% lower cost per bit and less dependence on new scanners.

title: 1970s ceramic hermetic packaging revived: corrosion-proof memory for free-air cooling
idea: Military DRAMs of the 1970s sat in hermetic ceramic (CERDIP) packages that kept moisture and sulfur out. DIMMs and HBM packages get ALD alumina/parylene stacks or glass-frit hermetic lids plus silver-free, sulfur-resistant contacts, so memory survives unconditioned outside air (high humidity, sulfur creep corrosion) and facilities can cool with direct outside air without humidification.
why: Water: direct free-air cooling without evaporative humidity control uses ~0 L/kWh (>10x vs evaporative), and corrosion plus humidity-driven leakage are the memory failure modes that block it today.

title: Cryo-control DRAM: shallow capacitors because 77 K kills leakage
idea: Quantum-computer control electronics run at 4-77 K, where subthreshold and junction leakage fall by ~10^6 and retention stretches to hours. Design a die that only runs in liquid nitrogen, with 0.5-1 fF capacitors (AR ~10 or planar) and no refresh circuitry, for sealed LN2-immersion AI racks. Reliability comes from temperature instead of capacitor height.
why: Removes the AR 60-75 capacitor and refresh (facts 1, 3): a ~5-6x shorter capacitor etch and fewer steps. The cost is LN2 cooling energy, partly offset by lower wire resistance and leakage.

title: Decay-direction coding: store mostly safe bits, detect with Berger
idea: Ideal: data that cannot decay. Closest: each word is stored inverted (with a flag bit) whenever that leaves fewer cells in the leaky charged state; rows that end up fully discharged skip refresh, and because the remaining errors are unidirectional (charged to discharged only) a cheap Berger count code detects every one of them.
why: Fact 3: halves worst-case leaky bits, skips refresh on sparse rows and swaps SECDED for ~log2(n) check bits.

title: Zero dies scrapped: AI-tolerant DRAM grade for out-of-spec dies
idea: Imposed limit: no die may be scrapped for retention or margin. Create a new JEDEC-like grade specified at 16 ms retention and BER 1e-8 that requires system-level ECC, recompute or ABFT. It is sold at a ~40% discount into inference clusters whose software stacks tolerate it.
why: Raises usable supply by the 5-15% yield gap at zero capex and relieves the shortage immediately.

title: Quantum erasure conversion: sense amps flag low-margin bits as erasures
idea: Neutral-atom quantum computers convert errors into erasures at known locations. Borrow that by adding a second, offset-threshold comparator to each sense amp, so any bit whose bitline differential falls below ~40 mV is flagged 'uncertain' and sent to the controller as a per-burst erasure mask on an extra pin. The controller runs erasure-aware Reed-Solomon decoding, which corrects about twice as many erasures as unknown errors for the same parity.
why: Retention-tail and VRT cells read with low margin before they actually flip. Erasure decoding lets the same 12.5% parity tolerate ~2x the raw weak-cell rate, which permits ~15-20% smaller Cs or 2-4x longer refresh (facts 1, 3).

title: Alien's indifference to testing: fountain-coded tiles across untested printed foil
idea: An alien never inspects parts one at a time: data is spread with a rateless (Raptor-style) code over many small printed memory tiles, and the controller reads tiles in parallel and stops as soon as any k good symbols decode, so dead or flaky tiles that were never tested or mapped simply don't contribute.
why: Removes per-tile test and repair cost and yield loss for printed memory (test can exceed 30% of its cost), tolerating 10-20% dead tiles at ~25% redundancy.

title: Epidemic contact tracing: ECC events trigger blast-radius refresh
idea: Epidemiologists trace and test the contacts of each case. When row r reports a corrected error, controller firmware treats it as a case. It immediately refreshes and scrubs r+-1..+-4 using the physical adjacency map. If more cases appear, it raises local refresh and asks the OS to quarantine (remap) the hot aggressor pages.
why: Free ECC events become hammer and weak-cell sensors (facts 3 and 9), and stop cascades before they reach uncorrectable errors. It needs firmware and a kernel hook only.

title: Three nested codes sized to relax cell BER to 1e-6
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting (Matryoshka): inner on-die SEC per 128 bits fixes scattered bits, a middle cross-device symbol code per cache line fixes dead mats/chips, and an outer controller-side XOR erasure code across each 4 KB page group (invoked only on rare uncorrectables) rebuilds whole lines; budgets are co-designed so raw cell BER can be 1e-6 instead of ~1e-12.
why: A ~10^6x relaxed raw error target permits ~25-35% smaller Cs (attacks the 4.5-5.4 fF charge wall) or 4-8x longer refresh at ~15% total parity.

title: Subsea-repeater cold spare: an unpowered extra die per stack
idea: Undersea cable repeaters carry unpowered cold spares through a 25-year unserviceable life. Add one unpowered DRAM die to each HBM/3DS stack, with a base-die crossbar that moves a degrading die's contents to the spare and remaps its channels once its corrected-error rate crosses a threshold. Powered-off silicon accumulates no BTI, hot-carrier or hammer stress.
why: Stacks can ship with lower-margin dies, and end-of-life die failures become transparent swaps. That raises effective HBM stack yield and lifetime by ~10-20% for ~6-12% extra silicon (fact 6).

title: Melt-pool-style monitoring: test each 3D tier before it is buried
idea: Metal 3D printers watch every layer's melt pool; after each 3D-DRAM tier is patterned, scan it with e-beam voltage-contrast inspection (no xenon plasma FIB or rare-gas plasma) to map opens and shorts, and program that tier's remap into antifuses or a base-die table before the next tier covers it.
why: Tier defects compound over 26+ tiers (fact 2); knowing them in-line lets the stack repair instead of scrap, flattening 3D yield loss.

title: Reactor-style self-anneal: on-die heaters heal leakage-tail traps
idea: Radiation-damaged detectors and fusion-reactor sensors are recovered by thermal annealing. Embed polysilicon heater lines in the periphery stripes of each bank. During a scheduled window, after the bank's data has been migrated away, the heaters hold the array at ~250 C for minutes to passivate the interface and oxide traps that create GIDL and VRT tail cells. An on-die tail monitor decides when a bank needs annealing.
why: Tail leakage cells (≤13 fA) set the 64 ms refresh. Periodically resetting the aging-driven growth of the tail could keep refresh intervals 2-4x longer over life and cut in-field weak-cell repairs (fact 3).

title: Run legacy-node U.S. DRAM at 77 K to erase tails
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar at 77 K | sense: standard | integration: liquid-nitrogen-cooled memory sled | substrate: bulk | fab: 25-30 nm DUV legacy process]. Junction and GIDL leakage fall >1000x at 77 K, so retention moves from 64 ms to minutes and weak tail cells become strong; older, EUV-free nodes with bigger, cheaper cells then serve disaggregated LN2-cooled memory racks.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: no EUV, refresh (16-33% of idle power) nearly disappears; cooling overhead offsets about half of the energy gain.

title: Memory leasing with telemetry-driven swap and refurbishment
idea: Rule: the maker keeps ownership, so repairability is its own profit motive. Memory is leased by GB-month, and the vendor monitors error telemetry, swaps degrading modules proactively, then refurbishes and redeploys them, which rewards designs that last.
why: Aligns the business model with longevity. Each module serves 2-3 deployments, which multiplies supply per wafer.

title: Pointer high-bit checksums catch flips without ECC chips
idea: Po: pointers that know where they should point. The compiler and runtime store a 12-16-bit checksum of each 48-bit pointer in its unused upper bits, checked on dereference by a cheap instruction; corrupted pointers trap and are reloaded from a replica.
why: Most catastrophic memory-error crashes are corrupted pointers; lets cheaper non-ECC DRAM serve more servers with crash rates closer to ECC parts.

title: Data-parallel training: model replicas become each other's ECC
idea: In a 10,000-GPU job, every data-parallel rank holds identical weights. Periodically checksum each 2 MB weight shard, compare checksums across replicas over NVLink or InfiniBand, and repair any mismatched shard by copying it from a majority peer. Local HBM errors are then corrected by replication that already exists.
why: Weights are ~30-50% of training HBM. Cross-replica voting gives TMR-like protection for free and lets weight regions run on weaker dies or relaxed refresh (facts 3, 6).

title: Lost-foam air gaps between buried wordlines via oxygen ash
idea: Lost-foam casting burns out a foam pattern to leave a cavity; deposit a carbon or polymer spacer between buried wordlines, cap it with porous oxide, then burn it out with an O2 ash (no argon sputter or plasma), leaving vacuum gaps that cut wordline-to-wordline and passing-gate coupling.
why: Lower coupling could raise the row-hammer threshold ~3-10x (fact 9) and cut wordline capacitance and energy (fact 10), all without rare gases.

title: Eliminate stored parity: decode weights against their known statistical prior
idea: Drop the 12.5% ECC parity for frozen model weights. The controller instead runs maximum-a-posteriori correction using the known per-tensor distribution of bf16/fp8 values (exponents cluster in a ~6-value window; signs and mantissas follow measured histograms), and repairs implausible words. A tiny CRC per 4 KB only confirms the fix.
why: Recovers ~12.5% capacity and tolerates raw BER ~1e-6 from cheaper, weaker cells on the weight tier; cost per usable bit falls ~10-15%.

title: Magnify scrub rate with one tiny patrol engine per panel tile
idea: Put a tiny patrol-scrub engine in each of thousands of panel tiles. It reads, corrects and rewrites its tile every ~100 ms, far faster than DRAM's one scrubber per die, so a single-bit error is fixed before a second lands in the same codeword.
why: Self-healing: uncorrectable rate scales as (error rate x scrub interval)^2, so 100x faster scrubbing tolerates ~100x higher error arrival with simple SEC-DED.

title: Chocolate-tempering anneal cycles for capacitor dielectric phase purity
idea: Chocolatiers cycle temperature so that only the stable Form V crystals survive. The ZrO2/HfO2 capacitor dielectric would get a cycled RTP profile: above the phase transition, cooled to nucleate, then reheated just below the melt point of the unstable phases. This dissolves the minority monoclinic and amorphous pockets and the vacancy-rich grain boundaries that make up the leakage tail.
why: A narrower leakage distribution could mean ~10x fewer weak cells and possibly k toward 45-50. Both relax the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the retention tail.

title: Mo: grounded molybdenum shield fins screen buried-wordline passing-gate coupling
idea: Insert a thin grounded Mo fin between adjacent buried wordlines, electrostatically screening the passing-gate field that modulates neighbor channels and storage-node junctions; Mo also replaces some tungsten (an 80%-China chokepoint) and is mined in the U.S.
why: Attacks the passing-gate row-hammer mechanism (fact 9) and GIDL tail (fact 3) at the source; target 5x higher hammer threshold.

title: Segment-aligned ECC codewords enable 64-bit micro-activations
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: segmented local wordline | sense: local sense per 72-cell segment | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Only one 64+8-bit segment of a row is raised and the whole ECC codeword lives inside that segment, so small accesses keep full SECDED protection and hammer disturbance and counters are confined to segment neighbours.
why: Constraint/Fact 8: removes the ~128x page overfetch, ~10-30x lower activation energy per useful bit, and shrinks hammer exposure per access.

title: Cochlear amplifier: Hopf-poised sense amp hears sub-femtofarad cells
idea: Cochlear hair cells sit at a Hopf bifurcation, giving huge gain for faint sounds; bias each sense amplifier at the edge of oscillation with a calibrated negative-resistance loop so the tiny bitline perturbation of a ~1 fF cell tips it decisively, with per-amp calibration of the bifurcation point.
why: Capacitor charge wall: if 1-2 fF cells become readable, pillar AR can fall from 60-75:1 to ~15-20:1, cutting deposition/etch cost and opening lateral 3D capacitors.

title: Second-life DRAM: re-certify decommissioned server dies under strong ECC
idea: Worse: shred millions of 3-5 year old DIMMs while new bits cost 4x more. Flip: industrial lines recover modules from retired servers, run deep retention and hammer profiling, and resell them graded into tiers behind controllers with chipkill plus elastic refresh for cold or secondary memory pools.
why: Supply and scarce resources: part of the installed base (tens of exabytes) could return as CXL capacity tiers using zero new wafers.

title: NAND-style read-reference tracking keyed to time since refresh
idea: Adapted from NAND flash controllers that shift read thresholds as charge drifts: each mat holds a few dummy cells rewritten at every refresh; at read time a small comparator samples their decayed voltage and shifts the sense-amp reference so the decision threshold follows the leakage curve instead of sitting at a fixed VARY/2.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): a moving reference recovers ~30-40% of signal margin late in the refresh window, allowing 2-4x longer tREFI and cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and bandwidth loss proportionally.

title: Hammer-absorbing row cache intercepts repeated activations
idea: Po: the hammer hits a pillow. A small SRAM cache of 8-16 row buffers per bank inside the DRAM holds rows activated more than N times in a window; further ACTs to those rows are served from SRAM without raising the array wordline at all.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and activation energy: attackers cannot toggle the hot wordline; also cuts ACT energy for hot rows ~30%.

title: Xylem pit valves: self-isolating subarrays contain shorts and defects
idea: Xylem pit membranes seal an embolized conduit so water reroutes; give each subarray a small isolation switch and current monitor on its local wordline supply and precharge rail, so a wordline-bitline short or gross leaker trips and seals that subarray (remapped to a spare) instead of collapsing the whole bank's voltage.
why: Yield and capital: shorts that poison entire banks are a major yield killer at aggressive pitch; containment turns bank kills into ~0.1% capacity loss, raising yield several points per wafer.

title: Low-leak isolation switch halves bitlines for weak rows
idea: Inverts 'every row sees the full bitline capacitance': one Vt-adjust implant mask creates a low-leakage isolation transistor mid-bitline; near-half rows are read with the far half cut off, halving Cbl, and the controller maps weak or hot data to those rows.
why: ~2x sense signal and faster tRCD for mapped weak cells (facts 1, 3); extends tiered-latency DRAM into a reliability tier.

title: Charge-trap trimming raises threshold of only the leakiest transistors
idea: Worse: let the one-in-a-million leaky access transistor set refresh for the whole chip. Flip: include a thin Si3N4 trap layer in the access-gate stack; at test, cells flagged as leaky get a Fowler-Nordheim program pulse via their wordline and bitline that traps electrons and raises their Vt ~0.3 V, permanently pulling them out of the tail.
why: Fact 3: trimming the tail ~10x extends the refresh period 4x or more, using only Si, N and O.

title: Substitute one stable large MTJ with analog majority of tiny unstable MTJs
idea: Store each bit in 5 sub-15 nm MTJs in parallel, each with low thermal stability (fails ~1e-3/hour alone); reading the summed parallel resistance gives the majority, so the bit fails only if 3 of 5 flip (~1e-8/hour) and periodic scrub restores flips.
why: Write energy and density: low-barrier MTJs switch with ~5x less current and tiny transistors; retention comes from redundancy, not barrier height.

title: Bell Model V two-out-of-five revival: reference-free top-k sensing
idea: Bell Labs relay computers stored digits in 2-out-of-5 constant-weight codes so every word checked itself. Store each 64-bit word as a 68-cell constant-weight codeword with exactly 34 charged cells (C(68,34) is about 2^64.6); instead of comparing each cell to a fixed Vref, a winner-take-all network marks the 34 highest-voltage cells as charged, so uniform decay, temperature drift and plate noise cancel out.
why: Retention tail and voltage floor (facts 3, 10): data survive until cells swap rank, not until they cross Vref, allowing ~4-8x longer refresh or ~40% less Cs, for 6% cell overhead plus detection of any weight-changing error.

title: Write-hot pages on leaky rows: application writes become free refresh
idea: Combine the OS page allocator with per-row retention profiling: pages whose write interval is shorter than a row's measured retention are placed on weak rows, since every write restores full charge; those rows become refresh-exempt while a write-interval monitor guarantees the deadline, and only cold-data rows get nominal refresh.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): makes the weakest 1-5% of rows usable without remapping and skips their refresh, cutting refresh energy/bandwidth ~10-30% and recovering yield.

title: Diels-Alder reversible mold compound for intact die recovery
idea: Rule: the package must open without damaging the die. DRAM is encapsulated in a mold compound with thermally reversible Diels-Alder crosslinks that de-crosslink at ~150 C, so dies can be lifted intact from failed or retired packages for failure analysis, repair or repackaging.
why: Makes die-level recycling and failure analysis cheap. Recovered good dies add supply, and the root-cause loop for reliability shortens.

title: Noise-cancelling wordlines: opposite pulses neutralize neighbor disturbance
idea: Combine active noise cancellation with wordline drive: when a wordline rises, drivers inject a small, timed opposite-polarity pulse on its two neighbors, cancelling the capacitively coupled disturbance on victim access gates; amplitude is calibrated per array. Buildable in a university nanofab: TFT arrays driven by external pulse generators.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): reduces coupling-driven victim leakage, potentially raising the flip threshold several-fold without counters.

title: Memory that trades capacity for parity as it ages
idea: Rearrange the parity/data split over the product lifetime: modules start with ~2% parity, and as the error log shows a region degrading, the controller re-encodes it with a stronger code and hot-unplugs the freed pages from the OS, degrading gracefully instead of failing.
why: Extends module service life ~2x and lets fabs ship cells that are weaker at end of life; fewer replacements raise usable supply.

title: Socketed DRAM chiplets on a reusable multi-generation interposer
idea: Rule: memory dies must be replaceable without discarding logic. DRAM chiplets attach to an active interposer through anisotropic conductive film or micro-spring contacts instead of permanent bonds, so failed chiplets are swapped and the interposer and accelerator are reused across 2-3 memory generations.
why: Cuts scrap of expensive packages from a single memory failure. Interposer capital is amortized across generations.

title: Camera pixel: pinned storage-node junction suppresses 125 C generation leakage
idea: Automotive image sensors beat 125 C dark current with a p+ surface pinning layer; the same shallow pinning implant over the storage-node junction surface plus an STI-sidewall passivation liner removes surface-state generation, the dominant hot leakage term.
why: Sensors cut dark current ~10x this way; the cell leakage tail at 125 C could fall 3-10x, allowing normal 64 ms refresh at 125 C through 10 years.

title: Four-level cells in fat 180 nm capacitors rescued by soft ECC
idea: Ideal: twice the bits from the same old cell. Closest: 180 nm stacked capacitors hold ~25-30 fF, enough charge for 4 levels at ~250 mV spacing; store 2 bits per cell with a three-reference sense amp and absorb the higher raw error rate with a page-level soft-decision BCH code.
why: Density and U.S. manufacturability: doubles bits per mm2 on legacy US lines with zero EUV.

title: Z-channel asymmetric ECC matched to one-way charge loss
idea: Worse: use symmetric codes that spend parity guarding against discharged-to-charged flips that almost never happen. Flip: since leakage and hammering mostly drain charge, use asymmetric (Z-channel, Varshamov-type) codes with true/anti-cell-aware mapping, which correct t unidirectional errors with fewer check bits than symmetric BCH.
why: ECC overhead and weak-cell tolerance: ~30-40% fewer parity bits for the same protection, or ~2x correction at the same overhead, enabling relaxed refresh.

title: VCR dropout compensator revival: conceal faulty words in AI tensors
idea: VCRs hid tape dropouts by substituting the previous scan line from a delay line. The accelerator's memory controller keeps a map of known-bad or uncorrectable words in tensor memory and on access substitutes a predicted value (neighbouring element, channel mean, or zero for activations) instead of trapping or retrying, logging each event.
why: Water: lets AI-tensor DRAM from an all-dry, ~10x-lower-water fab ship without repair fuses or spare rows, because scattered point defects are concealed instead of repaired; ~10% less capacity and ECC overhead.

title: Write-coalescing plus start-gap rotation qualifies 1e11-endurance cells
idea: First-principles budget: a hot line can take ~2e11 writes in 5 years. An on-die 1 MB write-combining SRAM absorbs >95% of hot rewrites, and start-gap row rotation spreads the rest, so per-cell writes fall below 1e10.
why: Widens the capacitorless menu: charge-trap, volatile MRAM and ferroelectric cells with 1e11-1e12 endurance can serve as DRAM.

title: Hybrid-ARQ incremental-redundancy ECC with far-stored heavy parity
idea: Adapted from LTE/5G hybrid ARQ, where the first transmission carries a light code and extra parity is sent only if decoding fails: each 64 B line carries only a small inline detect-and-correct-one code, while a strong Reed-Solomon parity per 4 KB region lives in a separate low-traffic row group and is fetched only on the rare detected failure.
why: ECC overhead and data movement (facts 5, 8): common-case reads move ~1.5% overhead instead of 12.5% while still tolerating raw BER ~1e-5 from weaker cells, reclaiming ~10% bandwidth and ~8% capacity.

title: Elastic parity that grows as the chip ages
idea: Inverts 'ECC strength is fixed at design time': pages start with a light code (CRC+SEC); when a page's syndrome rate rises the controller allocates extra parity from a pooled spare region and re-encodes it with a stronger LDPC, spending protection only where wear and tail cells appear.
why: Average ECC overhead ~3% instead of 12.5% while weak or aged regions get >4x stronger protection; extends module service life.

title: Deep-space soft-decision decoding inside the DRAM sense amp
idea: Adapted from deep-space telemetry (Voyager/Mars links decode near the noise floor with soft-decision LDPC): each sense amp reports the bit plus a 2-bit confidence derived from its latch time-to-decision (measured by a shared counter), and an on-die LDPC decoder over 512-bit codewords uses those soft values. Ambiguous bits from half-charge cells are flagged and corrected rather than guessed.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): reading ~2-2.5 fF cells instead of 4.5-5.4 fF lets capacitor aspect ratio drop from 60-75:1 toward ~35:1, cutting etch/deposition cost; soft decoding buys ~2-3 dB effective margin over hard SECDED.

title: Row-buffer-wide long code computed over the full 8KB page
idea: Scale jump (64-bit word -> 8KB row): activation already latches the whole row into sense amps, so place a polar/LDPC code spanning the entire row and decode it in the row buffer during activation. The 128x overfetch becomes a reliability asset.
why: Parity overhead drops from 12.5% to ~3% while tolerating raw BER ~1e-4, enabling weaker or smaller cells and about 9% more capacity per die.

title: Vernier-select contacts absorb misregistration from solid-state interference lithography
idea: A machinist's vernier reads alignment from offset scales; pattern the periodic array with solid-state-laser interference lithography (quadrupled Nd:YAG, no excimer neon), print periphery contacts as a vernier set of offset candidates, and after test electrically select whichever candidate landed on each line.
why: Interference litho makes cheap, rare-gas-free gratings but registers poorly to separately patterned periphery; vernier selection turns overlay error into a fuse choice, cutting litho capital (fact 4).

title: 180 nm RAS hub chip lets leading-edge dies ship raw
idea: Ideal: the DRAM die is pure array and all reliability logic is free. Closest: a buffer chip built in a fully depreciated 180 nm US fab sits on each DIMM and performs page-level BCH, a bad-row remap CAM and hammer tracking for 8-16 dies, so memory makers can drop on-die ECC and ship dies through relaxed retention screens.
why: Facts 7 and 3 plus U.S. manufacturability: moves ~5-10% of die area off leading-edge silicon onto 180 nm tools and raises sellable yield.

title: V: VO2 phase-change thermal integrator flags hammered subarrays
idea: A doped VO2 sliver (insulator-metal transition tuned near 70 C) is thermally coupled to each subarray's local wordline driver; sustained high activation rates heat it through the transition, its resistance drop trips a sense line that forces targeted neighbor refresh, while normal traffic never heats it enough.
why: Analog, counter-free hammer-rate detection (fact 9) that costs no logic area; complements fine-grained trackers.

title: Cicada prime-period sampling so hammer patterns cannot phase-lock
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on 13- or 17-year cycles so predators cannot synchronize; run TRR sampling windows and victim-refresh slots on mutually prime, per-bank randomly reseeded periods (13/17/19/23 tREFI), so many-sided and half-double patterns that exploit fixed sampler cadence never phase-lock with all banks.
why: Row hammer: TRRespass-style bypasses exploit periodic samplers; prime-period scheduling restores probabilistic guarantees using only small LFSR state, avoiding the 2-5% area of growing trackers.

title: TCP congestion control for refresh: AIMD on correctable-error signals
idea: Adapted from TCP's additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease loop, which probes for capacity until packets drop: each bank's refresh interval is lengthened in small steps while on-die ECC reports zero corrections and halved immediately when the correction rate crosses a threshold, so refresh tracks the bank's real retention at its current temperature and age.
why: Refresh cost (fact 3): typical banks retain 4-10x longer than worst-case spec; a closed loop riding the ECC margin could cut refresh energy and bandwidth loss 50-80%, with ECC as the safety net against variable-retention cells.

title: Dual-mode HZO/ZrO2 capacitor: volatile bit with ferroelectric safety copy
idea: Combine a DRAM capacitor with a ferroelectric backup in one ALD stack: a paraelectric ZrO2 layer holds the normal volatile charge, while a thin Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 layer is polarized only by an occasional higher-voltage backup pulse; if charge decays or ECC flags the row, the FE polarization is read to restore it. Buildable in a university nanofab: ALD plus <=400 C anneal.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): enables very long refresh intervals with FE as fallback, while rare switching limits FE fatigue.

title: Lifetime-tagged allocation skips refresh for short-lived data
idea: Ideal: no refresh because data dies before it decays. Closest: allocators tag buffers with expected lifetime (activations, packets, frame buffers); rows holding only data due to be overwritten within the retention guarantee are excluded from refresh by a per-row skip bit set by the controller.
why: Fact 3: in AI and streaming workloads ~50% of rows hold data living <64 ms, so refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~50%.

title: Buried high-SRH recombination layer absorbs row-hammer electrons
idea: Part of the hammer disturbance is electrons injected by the aggressor that diffuse through the substrate to victim junctions. Implant a carbon- or gold-doped layer deep below the storage-junction depletion region, where short minority lifetime (<1 ns) kills the migrating electrons. Keeping it out of the depletion region avoids raising SRH generation leakage.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): could push the flip threshold from ~1k toward ~10k ACTs, with no controller logic.

title: Fleet-learned repair: OTA refresh and PPR updates by lot signature
idea: Rule: repair must reach modules already in the field. The vendor aggregates anonymized ECC logs from millions of modules, learns failure signatures per wafer lot, and pushes firmware updates that adjust refresh rates and run pre-emptive soft PPR on modules carrying the same lot ID before they fail.
why: Turns field reliability into a continuously improving software problem and cuts uncorrectable-error returns.

title: Leaky-bucket hammer counter: IGZO TFT integrator on each wordline
idea: Combine the networking leaky-bucket with the wordline driver: each activation pumps a fixed charge quantum through an IGZO TFT onto a small MIM capacitor, while a subthreshold TFT drains it with a ~32-64 ms time constant; crossing a threshold triggers neighbor refresh. Buildable in a university nanofab: sputtered IGZO, ALD gate oxide and MIM at <=350 C.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): replaces per-row SRAM counters/CAMs in the periphery (fact 7) with an analog device whose decay matches the refresh window, at near-zero storage cost.

title: Wordline doubles as heater for periodic in-situ trap annealing
idea: Combine Joule microheaters with the array wordlines: in maintenance windows, after data is moved to another subarray, current through Mo or TiN wordline segments heats the local array to ~200-300 C for microseconds to milliseconds, annealing hydrogen-related and interface traps that create leakage tails. Buildable in a university nanofab: patterned Mo/TiN lines over IGZO or Si TFT arrays.
why: Retention tail and aging (fact 3): lifetime self-healing could tighten the tail 2-5x; also avoids tungsten wordlines (China ~80% chokepoint).

title: Self-referencing rows: decaying reference cells set the read threshold
idea: Combine reference cells with the data row: each row carries a '1' and a '0' reference cell written with the data, so they decay alongside it; the sense threshold is set at the midpoint of their residual levels, letting partially leaked data resolve correctly. Buildable in a university nanofab: TFT/MIM test arrays with an off-chip comparator.
why: Retention (fact 3): reads tolerate ~2x more charge loss, allowing ~2x longer refresh or smaller Cs, robust to temperature swings.

title: NEMS relay access switch: air-gap off-state ends leakage tail
idea: Combine a nanoelectromechanical relay with a storage capacitor: a released TiN or poly-Si seesaw relay replaces the access transistor, so the off-state is an air gap with essentially zero leakage and retention is limited only by the capacitor dielectric. Buildable in a university nanofab: sacrificial oxide released by vapor HF, e-beam defined gaps.
why: Access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3): could stretch retention to minutes and remove most refresh; risk is contact endurance (~1e15 cycles needed) and switching speed.

title: 2D-heterojunction tunnel-diode pair makes a self-holding capacitor cell
idea: Combine Esaki tunnel-diode bistability (the 1990s TSRAM concept) with van der Waals heterojunctions: two series BP/MoS2 or WSe2/SnSe2 negative-differential-resistance diodes latch the storage node at one of two stable points with picoamp standby current, so the cell needs no refresh. Buildable in a university nanofab: flake transfer plus e-beam patterning.
why: Eliminates refresh energy and retention tail (fact 3) in a DRAM-like cell; risks are peak-to-valley ratio and uniformity.

title: Solar-cell recombination layer between cells absorbs hammer electrons
idea: Combine the defect-rich recombination junctions of tandem solar cells with DRAM isolation: line the gap between adjacent storage nodes with a thin, deliberately defective a-Si or heavily doped poly film that recombines electrons injected from the hammered row before they reach the victim node. Buildable in a university nanofab: PECVD/LPCVD film on paired-node test structures.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attacks the charge-migration mechanism directly, potentially raising the flip threshold ~10x with no controller logic.

title: Sacrificial-polymer air gaps between wordlines cut hammer coupling
idea: Combine BEOL air-gap interconnect with DRAM wordlines: fill wordline gaps with a thermally decomposable polymer (polynorbornene or polycarbonate), cap with PECVD oxide and bake so the polymer diffuses out, leaving air gaps that cut line-to-line capacitance ~50%. Buildable in a university nanofab: spin-coat, PECVD and bake.
why: Row hammer and wordline energy (facts 9, 10): reduces capacitive disturbance coupled into neighbor rows and CV^2 wordline energy.

title: ReRAM soft-fuse table in BEOL enables lifelong self-repair
idea: Combine filamentary ReRAM (sputtered TaOx/HfOx between TiN electrodes) with the redundancy fuse bank: repair addresses live in a reprogrammable BEOL ReRAM array above the periphery, so the chip remaps newly failing rows in the field and can undo mistakes, replacing one-time laser/e-fuses. Buildable in a university nanofab: sputter plus two lithography layers.
why: Self-healing and periphery area (facts 3, 7): lifetime repairs cut field failure rates and free fuse area.

title: Inkjet-printed oxide memory made usable by heavy LDPC coding
idea: Combine solution-processed, inkjet-printed In-Zn-O TFT plus capacitor arrays (maskless, <300 C) with strong LDPC and spare-block mapping, so arrays with 1e-3 defect/BER rates still deliver error-free storage. Buildable in a university nanofab: a printer, hotplate and probe station.
why: Capital intensity and EUV (fact 4): tool cost drops by orders of magnitude; density is far lower, so it targets cheap capacity tiers and proves defect-tolerant design.

title: Test-then-write: maskless e-beam final metal routes around defects
idea: Combine wafer test with maskless lithography: after electrical test of the cell array, a per-die e-beam (or laser direct-write) exposure of the final metal layer is computed so bitline/wordline straps bypass defective cells and segments, giving every die custom wiring. Buildable in a university nanofab: e-beam writer plus probe-station test.
why: Yield and redundancy area (facts 4, 7): replaces built-in spare rows and fuses with per-die wiring; with multi-beam writers in production it raises yield of immature 3D or new-material arrays.

title: Kelvin-probe imaging maps thousands of cell retention curves in parallel
idea: Combine Kelvin probe force microscopy with retention testing: fabricate arrays with exposed storage-node pads, write them, then time-lapse map surface potential across thousands of nodes to extract full leakage distributions and the spatial correlation of tail cells without per-cell probing. Buildable in a university nanofab: standard AFM/KPFM tool.
why: Retention-tail learning loop (fact 3): makes 1e-4 to 1e-6 tail statistics affordable for new-material cells, speeding tail-reduction R&D.

title: Hydrogen-getter cap layer stabilizes oxide-channel access transistor tails
idea: Combine Ti/Pd hydrogen-getter films from vacuum packaging with oxide-semiconductor access transistors: a patterned getter layer above the passivation absorbs mobile hydrogen that would otherwise drift into the channel and shift threshold voltage, narrowing the leakage and drift tail. Buildable in a university nanofab: sputtered metal and one lithography step.
why: Leakage tail and drift (fact 3): a tighter Vth distribution lowers the off-current tail and permits longer refresh.

title: Canary patch with thinned dielectric acts as self-timed refresh clock
idea: Combine canary cells with an oscillator: each subarray holds a few cells with a deliberately leakier, thinner dielectric patch, and their decay crossing triggers that subarray's refresh, automatically tracking temperature, aging and process instead of a fixed worst-case timer. Buildable in a university nanofab: one extra lithography step and a thinner ALD deposition.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): replaces one worst-case interval with locally tracked ones, cutting refresh ~2-4x at moderate temperatures.

title: Open-PDK shuttle CMOS plus university BEOL cell post-processing
idea: Combine open-source SKY130/GF180 shuttle chips carrying sense amps, ECC and refresh controllers with university post-processing of capacitor or oxide-TFT arrays on the top-metal pads, giving full-stack reliability testbeds (real arrays plus real ECC) for a few tens of thousands of dollars. Buildable in a university nanofab: low-temperature BEOL steps on diced shuttle die.
why: Speeds iteration on reliability schemes for new cells (facts 2, 3) and builds US memory know-how; a strategy rather than a cell.

title: Dielectric-absorption reservoir: slow polarization refills leaking storage node
idea: Combine dielectric absorption (soakage, normally a capacitor flaw) with DRAM: a bilayer of fast linear dielectric plus a slow-relaxing defect-dipole layer (Nb- or La-doped ZrO2) releases polarization charge back onto the node over milliseconds after a write, offsetting junction leakage and flattening the decay curve. Buildable in a university nanofab: ALD doping supercycles.
why: Charge wall and retention (facts 1, 3): adds effective storage at long timescales without fast capacitance; speculative ~2x retention.

title: Laser-trim healing: test, then locally anneal each leaky cell
idea: Combine laser trimming of analog resistors with retention test: after mapping tail cells, a focused laser pulse locally anneals each leaky cell's junction or channel to passivate the defect, or deliberately opens it so it is mapped out. Buildable in a university nanofab: laser writer plus probe-station retention map.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): targeted repair of the ~1e-5 tail could double the refresh interval; production needs fast galvo systems.
